props.title: Klute
props.initialSlug: Private eye stalks killer to protect call girl

sections.content: Klute revolutionized the neo-noir thriller by masterfully blending psychological character study with paranoid surveillance culture. Jane Fonda's Oscar-winning performance as call girl Bree Daniels set new standards for complex female characterization in American cinema. Director Alan J. Pakula crafts a suffocating atmosphere of urban isolation that would influence his later paranoia trilogy entries The Parallax View (1974) and All the President's Men (1976). The film's exploration of voyeurism and power dynamics predates similar themes in Blue Velvet (1986) and The Conversation (1974).

sections.content: Gordon Willis's revolutionary cinematography in Klute established a visual template for urban paranoia that influenced decades of thrillers. His use of negative space and shadow transformed New York City into a labyrinth of threat and surveillance. This visual style directly influenced later films like Taxi Driver (1976) and Eyes of Laura Mars (1978), where the city itself becomes an antagonistic presence. The claustrophobic framing and emphasis on watching/being watched created a new visual language for psychological thrillers.

The film's exploration of female autonomy through Bree Daniels remains groundbreaking. Unlike exploitation films of the era, Klute presents sex work with complexity and humanity. This sophisticated approach influenced later character studies like Looking for Mr. Goodbar (1977) and American Gigolo (1980), though few matched Fonda's nuanced portrayal of professional and personal independence. sections.content: Klute established crucial elements of surveillance noir that would define the genre through the 1970s and beyond. The film's focus on recorded conversations and hidden observation predates similar themes in The Conversation (1974) and Blow Out (1981). Modern surveillance thrillers like Enemy of the State (1998) and Gone Girl (2014) continue to build on Pakula's pioneering exploration of technology, privacy, and power.
